title: Special tributes ahead of Elche v Barça - FC Barcelona
content: The applause rang out ahead of the Elche v FC Barcelona match. All eyes were on Marcial Pina and the blaugrana 2026 World Cup winners with Spain before Hansi Flick's side made their LaLiga bow. Marcial Pina, the former blaugrana and Elche player received an emotional tribute on his 80th birthday today. The event took place on the pitch at the Martínez Valero stadium once both sides had warmed up. FC Barcelona president Joan Laporta gave him a jersey with the name ‘MARCIAL’ and the number 10 on the back. A very special moment he could share with his five grandchildren too. Marcial Pina played for Barça from 1969 to 1977. Known as the Ros d’Or, the Asturian played in midfield and attack, and was part of one of the all-time great forward lines alongside Rexach, Asensi, Cruyff and Sotil. He was known for his technical ability and intelligent play. A really class player who was admired by all and made football look easy. He had also played for Elche, which made the game today even more special for the footballer. The tribute to Marcial Pina was a standout moment pre-match, but another was yet to come before kick-off, as Elche acknowledged the seven World Cup winners at the Martínez Valero stadium. Joan Garcia, Lamine Yamal, Gavi, Pedri, Eric, Olmo and Cubarsí all received a commemorative plaque from the home side. A real sporting gesture that was met with great applause from the Elche players and those present in the stadium.

title: Norway's King Harald V health worsens amid blood infection - Türkiye Today
content: The health of King Harald V of Norway, 89, has deteriorated over the weekend while he remains hospitalized for complications tied to a blood condition, the Norwegian royal palace said in a statement Sunday. Harald, Europe's oldest reigning monarch, is being treated for haemolytic anaemia, a disorder in which red blood cells are destroyed faster than the body can replace them, producing fatigue, paleness and shortness of breath. "His Majesty the King's health deteriorated over the weekend," the palace said. It added that the king "is receiving antibiotics for a bacterial infection in his blood and has responded to this treatment." Harald was admitted to Oslo University Hospital on Monday after developing fluid retention linked to the cortisone treatment he has been receiving for the anaemia. He was placed on sick leave for two weeks. The palace had earlier said the king had canceled a planned visit to the central Trondelag region, scheduled for September 1 and 2, which would have fallen after the initial sick-leave period was set to end. Harald ascended the Norwegian throne in 1991. He has faced repeated health problems in recent years but has consistently ruled out abdicating. Several family members, including Crown Prince Haakon, who is serving as regent during his father's hospitalization, have visited him in the hospital. The king's declining health comes amid broader turmoil for Norway's royal household. Crown Princess Mette-Marit, Haakon's wife, has faced scrutiny over her ties to the late Jeffrey Epstein, the American financier and convicted sex offender. Separately, Mette-Marit's son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Hoiby, was sentenced in June to four years in prison on two rape convictions and 32 other charges, including violence against a former partner. He has appealed the verdict. Despite the strain, the royal family continues to enjoy broad popularity among Norwegians.

title: The Used Luxury SUV That Makes A New CR-V Look Expensive - Top Speed
content: The Honda CR-V is one of the safer bets in the compact-SUV market, but demand has caused its prices to climb the MSRP ladder to the point that newer-model-year used options have become viable considerations. The range-topping 2026 Sport Touring Hybrid, for example, clocks in at $42,550, with standard all-wheel drive, leather seating, premium audio, and a 204-horsepower dual-motor hybrid powertrain. In all fairness, that is a lot of sensible SUV for the money, but it costs enough to warrant a look at compact luxury SUV models that have recently come on the used-car market. A buyer willing to look at two-, three-, four- or five-year-old vehicles will find luxury-brand SUVs for about the same price, having depreciation do the bulk of the price-equality work. Depreciation is the great equalizer in the used-car market, and it is relentless when it comes to luxury vehicles. Buyers who wouldn’t chance a glance at a $60,000-plus luxury SUV even a couple years ago can consider it instead of the mainstream SUV that fits comfortably into their monthly budget. Luxury SUVs depreciate more quickly because of their high purchase prices and rapid technology upgrades. The average vehicle loses about 40 to 50 percent of its value over its first five years, with luxury vehicles at the top end of that range. For comparison, SUVs are about in the middle of that range, and luxury SUV depreciation ranges from 45 to 55 percent, and about 30 to 35 percent over its first two years. Working backwards with that math, a $42,550 2026 Honda CR-V (the top-of-the-line Sport Touring Hybrid) carries a price equivalent to a 2023 $65,000 luxury SUV. At $42,550, the 2026 Honda CR-V Sport Touring Hybrid sits justifiably at the top of the CR-V lineup, with a standard equipment list that includes a 204-horsepower two-motor hybrid system, standard AWD, a five-mode drive selector, 19-inch gloss-black alloy wheels, leather-trimmed seats (heated in front), heated steering wheel, power sunroof, and dual-zone climate control. That price and level of standard equipment brings the 2026 Honda CR-V Sport Touring Hybrid to the borderline of luxury-SUV territory, combining the CR-V's everyday practicality with a distinctly upscale feature set. There is no mistaking it as a premium compact SUV (and a really good one, at that), though the mindset still remains with some buyers that it is just a gussied-up econobox SUV on which you compromise because you can’t afford the luxury compact SUV you really desire. Age needs context. A 2022 luxury SUV is not necessarily an old SUV in 2026. Some five-year-old models may still be on the current generation cycle, meaning the looks and mechanicals are still the same, and even some of the technology (though that sometimes changes dramatically from year to year). Barring mid-cycle refreshes, basic design, cabin architecture, safety features, and powertrain usually carry over. Even with mid-cycle refreshes, some luxury-SUV things don’t change. Buyers may have to accept that the technology has been upgraded over five years (sometimes overhauled), but carefully selected 2022–2025 SUVs still have contemporary driver-assistance systems, modern digital displays, premium audio systems, and contemporary comfort and convenience features. Take this standout that combines a prestigious badge, top-notch amenities and a high-performance powertrain. The 2022 BMW X3 M40i illustrates the benefits of depreciation particularly well, in terms of dollar value. Its original MSRP was $57,800 and Kelley Blue Book’s current Fair Purchase Price is listed at $39,400, translating into a depreciation of 32 percent (which isn’t at all bad for a four-year-old luxury compact SUV, as noted above). Further, KBB predicts a private party purchase price of $37,000, all depending on condition. The M40i’s average used-market value has genuinely moved it into new-CR-V territory, particularly if you’re comparing this top-tier model to the top-tier 2026 Honda CR-V Sport Touring Hybrid. There is a caveat, though. Depreciation does not work on the BMW’s premium-car running costs. A luxury SUV continues to warrant luxury pricing for insurance, maintenance, repairs and parts. And there’s the added cost of premium fuel for top performance. Against the 2026 Honda CR-V Sport Touring Hybrid, the 2022 BMW X3 M40i's biggest advantage lies under the hood. Its 3.0-liter turbocharged inline-six produces 382 horsepower and 369 pound-feet of torque, and you can get an extra 11-horsepower boost from the engine’s mild hybrid system. It uses an eight-speed automatic transmission to send power to all four wheels using the standard xDrive AWD system, and includes adaptive M Suspension, variable sport steering and performance control. Acceleration to 60 mph is rated by BMW at 4.4 seconds and listed by various sources in the 4.1–4.2-second range. However, it prefers premium fuel, though regular is acceptable and premium is recommended for top performance, and its fuel economy is rated by the EPA at just 23 mpg combined, which borders on big-engine guzzling. The X3 M40i is a performance compact that happens to have five seats and useful cargo space. The side benefit of choosing the 2022 BMW X3 M40i over a 2026 Honda CR-V is the expected, and sometimes innovative, luxury-SUV treatment—powered sport front seats with lumbar adjustment and thigh extensions, panoramic sunroof, three-zone climate control, keyless entry, power tailgate, premium sound system, and a comprehensive suite of driving aids. Its interior room and versatility are compact-SUV average, with seating for five, 101.4 cubic feet of passenger volume, and 28.7 cubic feet of cargo space (expandable to 62.7). Seating is upright and airy, with about 40 inches of headroom, and 36.7 inches of rear-seat legroom. As you'll discover later, it's smaller than the 2026 CR-V, but hardly a compromised sport sedan wearing an SUV body style. Imagine time-traveling between automotive timelines, in which the current Honda CR-V Sport Touring Hybrid is visited by a BMW X3 M40i from the past. The two were never meant to occupy the same economic universe, but the warping of the space/time continuum means the four-year-old BMW X3 is able to compete on equal footing with the present-day Honda CR-V. Pitting the speed, mechanical sophistication and luxury of the former against the latter’s efficiency, practicality and modern value creates an interesting dynamic. On paper, they look like visitors from entirely different galaxies. In the real-world battle of used versus new, however, they become worthy adversaries. Which one comes out on top? Let’s find out. The mechanical force between the 2022 BMW X3 M40i and 2026 Honda CR-V Sport Touring Hybrid are extremes of the same energy. The X3 M40i is aggressive and emotional, wielding 382 horsepower and 369 pound-feet of torque, an eight-speed transmission and performance tuned xDrive AWD to blast to 60 mph in a claimed 4.4 seconds. The CR-V Hybrid is peaceful and aims to stay in harmony with its environment, with a 204-horsepower 2.0-liter dual-motor hybrid powertrain and continuously variable transmission delivering EPA ratings of 40 mpg/34 mpg/37 mpg (city/highway/combined). Compact SUV battles, especially those involving family values, are fought in interior comfort, space and versatility. The BMW X3 M40i is bigger in overall footprint, but only marginally—an inch in overall length and width—and rides on a six-inch longer wheelbase, giving it a more stable stance from which to attack. Theoretically, it should have the larger interior, but the Honda counterstrikes with two more cubic feet of passenger volume, six inches more overall legroom, and 9.5 cubic feet more of cargo volume (expanding to nearly 14 more cubic feet when the rear seats are folded down). That gives the CR-V Hybrid the higher ground when the mission involves passengers, luggage and the real-world realities of family life. The X3's dark-side temptation starts to overpower its emotional appeal when you factor in the costs of ownership. Depending on region and demographics, the 2022 BMW X3 M40i carries an estimated five-year cost to own of between $72,000 and $79,000, according to Edmunds, including $11,000–$12,500 in projected maintenance and insurance in the $3,000–$7,500 range, as well as EPA-estimated annual fuel costs of $3,300. In contrast, the 2026 Honda CR-V Sport Touring Hybrid remains serene, with Edmunds' estimated costs ranging from $42,500 to $46,500, including a swing of $4,500 to $6,000 for maintenance and $2,400–$6,600 for insurance. The EPA projects annual fuel costs at $1,650, which is half that of the 2022 X3 and signifies a difference of $8,250 over five years of ownership. The takeaway is that depreciation has created a used market in which a $42,550 Honda CR-V budget can acquire a $60,000 BMW, though that vehicle has four years of real-world experience under its belt. The 2022 BMW X3 M40i makes a convincing argument against spending $42,550 on a 2026 Honda CR-V Sport Touring Hybrid, when you look at its expected sub-$40,000 purchase price. It’s especially relevant to buyers who want more oomph and to portray more prestige from their family-SUV purchase. You could argue, though, that real-world sensibilities and restraint portray a more family-friendly mindset with the CR-V Hybrid, with the latter proving to be the more rational long-term purchase, particularly for drivers who desire a more spacious and versatile interior, and rack up more miles in urban and suburban circles, rather than racing ovals. The comparison isn’t isolated, though, with other luxury SUVs offering consideration against the CR-V. For buyers who like the CR-V formula but want more luxury while keeping it in the family, the 2024 Acura RDX SH-AWD is worth consideration, especially when it's fitted with A-Spec and Advance packages. Its original MSRP was $54,150, and it’s currently fair-priced by KBB at $38,900. The platform is similar, but the differences are many—a 2.0-liter turbocharged "four," AWD, and a more premium cabin, but also an EPA-projected $3,300 fuel bill and a $54,000–$62,500 Edmunds True Cost-To-Own range. On the domestic side, the 2025 Cadillac XT4 Sport is available in the $39,400 range (according to KBB), down just over five percent from its original MSRP of $41,595, but that is the FWD model. Choosing the AWD model would drive the price beyond the 2026 CR-V ceiling, taking it to $47,500–$50,300 (according to J.D. Power). With the Cadillac, you also get a 2.0-liter turbocharged four-cylinder (rated at 225 horsepower) and a $63,000–$66,000 true cost to own over five years (around $4,500 on maintenance), but you don't spend as much on fuel as the other luxury compact SUV considerations (around $3,000 per year). title: Liverpool team news v Newcastle: Jacquet starts, Mac Allister a sub in Iraola’s first official game - Yahoo Sports
content: Andoni Iraola's reign as Liverpool head coach begins in earnest this afternoon as he takes charge of the Reds in a competitive fixture for the first time, with the Merseysiders beginning their 35th Premier League season away to Newcastle. It'll be an emotional occasion at St James' Park as both sets of fans pay tribute to the late, great Kevin Keegan – a legendary figure at these two clubs – who died 34 days ago. Iraola has been hired to mastermind a revival at Anfield after the misery of the 2025/26 campaign, although a mixture of good and bad results in pre-season and a quiet summer transfer window makes it hard to get a read on where exactly Liverpool are at right now. Today's opponents are also under new management in Matthias Jaissle and have lost some of their standout players from last season (Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali, Bruno Guimaraes), so an air of uncertainty hangs over both teams going into this fixture. Iraola has named his first starting XI for a competitive fixture as Liverpool head coach. Alisson Becker begins his ninth season with the Reds as the starting goalkeeper, with the similiarly experienced Virgil van Dijk partnered by summer arrival Jeremy Jacquet at centre-back. Jeremie Frimpong and Milos Kerkez occupy the full-back positions. Dominik Szoboszlai and Ryan Gravenberch start in midfield, with Florian Wirtz in the number 10 role. Cody Gakpo and Rio Ngumoha are on the flanks, with the latter back at the site of his fairytale Premier League debut, in which he scored a 100th-minute winner this time last year. Also back at St James' Park is Alexander Isak for his first return to the venue since his tempestuous transfer from Newcastle 12 months ago. No doubt the Swedish marksman will be subjected to a rather hostile reception on Tyneside today. Alexis Mac Allister is among the substitutes, alongside summer signings Victor Munoz and Ronald Araujo. The bench also includes young talents in Trey Nyoni, Lewis Koumas and James McConnell. title: The American V8 Sedan Built For Old-School Drivers - Top Speed
content: There is something increasingly unusual about a modern performance sedan that asks its driver to do some of the work. As the industry moves toward smaller turbocharged engines, electrification, all-wheel drive, and transmissions that shift faster than any human could, one American sedan continues to make a different argument. It does not need to reinvent the formula. Instead, it doubles down on the ingredients that made high-performance cars so compelling in the first place. A big V8, rear-wheel drive, a manual transmission, and enough power to overwhelm the rear tires. The result is a sedan that feels almost rebellious in an increasingly digital performance-car world. The engine is the first clue that this Cadillac was developed with a very different philosophy from most modern performance sedans. Under the hood sits a hand-built 6.2-liter supercharged V8, rather than a smaller twin-turbocharged six-cylinder or four-cylinder. It uses a cam-in-block architecture with two valves per cylinder, direct injection, and active fuel management. On premium gasoline, it produces 668 horsepower at 6,500 rpm and 659 pound-feet of torque at 3,600 rpm. Cadillac quotes a 0-to-60 mph time of just 3.4 seconds. Those numbers are important, but the way the engine produces them matters just as much. A supercharger delivers its boost differently from a turbocharger. There is no waiting for exhaust gases to build pressure before the engine responds. The result is an immediate, muscular connection between throttle input and acceleration. Press the accelerator and the V8 answers with a surge that feels linear, forceful and distinctly mechanical. Turbocharging has become the dominant solution for extracting more performance from smaller engines while improving efficiency and emissions. The regular CT5-V, for example, uses a 3.0-liter twin-turbocharged V6 producing 360 horsepower and 405 pound-feet. The Blackwing takes a completely different route, using twice the cylinders and more than twice the displacement per cylinder to deliver its performance. It is not the most efficient way to build a fast sedan. Cadillac itself rates the Blackwing at just 13 mpg city and 20 mpg highway. But efficiency was clearly not the primary objective here. The objective was character. The engine also gives the Blackwing an unmistakable soundtrack. The supercharged V8's induction noise, mechanical whine, and exhaust note combine to create an experience that simply cannot be replicated by a smaller turbocharged engine or an electric motor. That makes the Blackwing unusual before it even moves. The engine would already make the Blackwing special, but Cadillac went considerably further. Power is sent exclusively to the rear wheels, and the standard transmission is a six-speed manual. A 10-speed automatic is available, but the manual is the combination that best captures the philosophy behind this car. That matters because 668 horsepower is not a number that can simply be switched off by an electronic safety net. The driver has to manage it. The six-speed manual puts the driver directly into the process. Selecting the correct gear, judging engine speed, modulating the clutch and controlling throttle application become part of the experience. With 659 pound-feet available, there is always enough torque to punish a sloppy input, but that is also part of the appeal. Modern performance cars increasingly do an enormous amount of the thinking for their drivers. All-wheel-drive systems distribute torque between axles, dual-clutch transmissions execute near-instantaneous shifts and sophisticated stability systems intervene before mistakes become expensive. The Blackwing certainly has sophisticated electronics of its own. It features Performance Traction Management, an electronic limited-slip differential, launch control, Magnetic Ride Control, and selectable drive modes. Its Brembo brakes are designed to handle repeated hard use, while an available carbon-ceramic setup provides even greater stopping power. But those systems support the driver rather than replacing the experience. The rear-drive layout is particularly important. Instead of simply launching with all four tires clawing for traction, the Blackwing makes its rear axle an active participant in the driving experience. Throttle application can alter the car's attitude, and the driver can exploit the enormous grip available from its wide performance tires. The result is a sedan that can be driven quickly without feeling clinical. It feels like a machine. This is where the Blackwing stops being merely an interesting alternative and becomes something genuinely extraordinary. Cadillac gives the sedan 668 horsepower, 659 pound-feet of torque and a manufacturer-estimated 3.4-second sprint to 60 mph. It can exceed 200 mph on a racetrack, according to Cadillac. Those figures put the Blackwing firmly into super-sedan territory. Yet the most impressive part is not simply that it is fast. Plenty of modern sedans are brutally quick. The difference is that the Blackwing combines that speed with a package that remains unusually focused on driver involvement. Magnetic Ride Control continuously adapts the suspension, while the performance-oriented chassis, electronic limited-slip differential and Performance Traction Management system allow the car to transition between road-going comfort and serious track capability. The brakes are equally serious. Brembo hardware is fitted at both ends, with slotted performance rotors standard and carbon-ceramic brakes available for buyers who intend to spend significant time on a circuit. The car also rides on 19-inch forged wheels with high-performance tires, including 275-section rubber at the front and 305-section tires at the rear. That combination gives the Blackwing the hardware to exploit its engine rather than merely advertise it. And yet it remains a genuine sedan. There are five seats, 11.9 cubic feet of cargo space and a cabin designed to function as a luxury interior rather than a stripped-out race-car cockpit. Cadillac quotes 42.4 inches of front legroom and 37 inches of rear legroom. That dual personality is one of the Blackwing's greatest strengths. It can be a brutally fast driver's car on Saturday morning and still function as a reasonably practical luxury sedan during the week. For 2026, Cadillac lists the CT5-V Blackwing at $98,900 before options, putting it firmly into expensive territory but also making its mechanical specification remarkable for the money. Calling the Blackwing "old school" does not mean calling it primitive. Inside, the car is packed with technology. Cadillac offers heated and massaging front seats, a heated steering wheel, premium materials, carbon-fiber trim, and a 33-inch display with Google built-in. An AKG 16-speaker audio system is also available, while Super Cruise can provide hands-free driving assistance on compatible roads. That combination is important because the Blackwing does not reject modern luxury. It simply refuses to let technology become the entire personality of the car. The suspension can absorb ordinary road imperfections. The seats can provide the sort of comfort expected from a modern Cadillac. The technology can handle navigation, entertainment, and driver assistance. Then the driver presses the V button, selects a gear, and finds an entirely different machine underneath. That contrast is what makes the Blackwing so compelling. There is also something reassuringly physical about the controls. A manual shifter moves through a defined gate. A clutch pedal has to be operated. The engine responds to throttle position. The rear axle responds to power. The driver can feel the consequences of their decisions. That is increasingly unusual. Even some of the world's most accomplished performance sedans have moved toward turbocharged engines, automatic transmissions and all-wheel drive. Those cars are extraordinarily capable, often faster in the real world and easier to drive quickly. But they can also create a layer of separation between the person behind the wheel and the machine underneath. Calling any car the "last" of anything is risky. Automotive history rarely follows a perfectly predictable path. But the evidence makes the Blackwing's position increasingly difficult to ignore. The formula it represents is disappearing. A large-displacement supercharged V8 is already an increasingly unusual choice in a new performance sedan. A rear-wheel-drive layout is becoming less common as manufacturers pursue all-weather traction and increasingly sophisticated torque-vectoring systems. And a six-speed manual transmission has become almost exotic in the luxury performance segment. The Blackwing combines all three. More importantly, Cadillac is not merely keeping the configuration alive as a symbolic gesture. It continues to offer the 668-horsepower supercharged V8 with the six-speed manual for the 2026 model year. Cadillac lists the car as having extremely limited availability, while a special Curated by Cadillac version is being hand-built in Michigan with production beginning in mid-2026. That special model's approximately $158,000 starting price also demonstrates just how exclusive the formula can become. The company now sells electric performance models alongside combustion-powered V-Series cars, including the 519-horsepower Optiq-V and the electric Lyriq-V. The CT4-V Blackwing uses a twin-turbocharged V6 rather than a V8, while the CT5-V Blackwing remains the flagship expression of Cadillac's traditional high-output formula. That broader industry shift makes the Blackwing more significant. The argument is not that electric or turbocharged performance cars are worse. In many measurable respects, they are faster, more efficient and more technologically advanced. The argument is that the Blackwing represents a type of car that is becoming harder to build under modern efficiency, emissions, and electrification pressures. A 6.2-liter supercharged V8 powering the rear wheels through a manual transmission is almost an act of defiance. And that is why the Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing matters to enthusiasts. It is a reminder that performance is not defined solely by acceleration numbers. title: The V-Twin That Quietly Became The Smart Buy - Top Speed
content: Abhik has been an automotive journalist for over 14 years, with expertise in both motorcycle and car road testing, reviewing, as well as writing and executing feature travelogs. He has worked for Indian brands including Evo India Magazine, Auto Today by India Today Group, and anchored video reviews for Powerdrift Studios. He also has keen interests in most forms of motorsports, having competed in a couple of seasons of one-make racing with TVS Racing on two wheels and Volkswagen Motorsport on four. Alongside his motoring pursuits, e-sports and sim racing are current interests, as are cycling and cycling tech. The 645cc V-twin powering the SV650 since 1999 didn't get retired when Suzuki built a newer 776cc engine in 2023, and now it's doing something new. There isn't much technology exchange between cars and motorcycles, since just about everything in the two-wheeled world has to be engineered differently, but tech crosses over occasionally on newer bikes. Not that the V-twin engine is going to make an appearance in any car anytime soon (or ever), but it’s the segment name that, well, crossed over. Suzuki Cycles' website now files this old but capable V-twin under a term borrowed straight from cars, "Crossover." And this new machine is a really smart buy in its segment. As the word suggests, when a certain body type crosses over into another, a crossover is born. As much as that sounds weirdly PG-18, in car terms, it’s a fusion of, say, a sedan and an SUV or, more commonly, a hatchback and an SUV. Best of both worlds and master of none, you might argue, but there’s a solid global demand backing up this type of vehicle. Motorcycling adopted the label as well as the same philosophy. Adventure bike outlook with sport bike underpinnings and cycle parts. What’s not to love here? This is why the popularity of such bikes is rising. Triumph, Honda, Suzuki, Yamaha, and BMW all have players in this crossover space, some even boasting multiple bikes. Things narrow down when you bring 'V-twin' into the mix, though. In fact, there's only one true V-twin crossover right now, which is single-handedly taking the fight to inline-triple or parallel-twin rivals. It does that by offering stunning value in this heated space. Suzuki’s Crossover lineup has two bikes, and the 2027 SV-7GX is the newest kid on the block. In essence, it’s the modern version of an idea Suzuki tried a long time ago and shelved. Back in 1997, the XF650 Freewind was a mixed dual-sport running gear with street-leaning bodywork. A bike way ahead of its time, even before the term crossover was coined, and it never made it past Europe. The SV-7GX finishes what the Freewind started back then, right when this category is ripe with contenders. And the value aspect comes from its starting price of $8,599, or $8,399 for the graphics-free trim, the SV-7GXV. Interestingly, the value proposition even extends to the motor, as it packs a reliable champ of an engine that has powered the SV650 and the V-Strom 650. For the SV-7GX, Suzuki had a newer engine sitting right there. The 776cc parallel-twin that powers the GSX-8R and S launched just a year apart from each other. With a newer bottom end and a 270-degree crank tuned for a broader spread of power, plus making meeting emission standards easier, reaching past it for the 645cc V-twin that's been around since 1999 seems like a step backward. But it’s the pricing that’s a bigger factor, at which point Suzuki’s decision starts looking deliberate. The 90-degree V-twin still makes 72.4 horsepower at 8,500 rpm and 47.2 lb-ft at 6,800 rpm, as well as packing the SV650’s reliability, but the output is really not the point here. Suzuki picking this engine hints at existing tooling for it. Twenty-seven years of production means the casting molds, the emissions certification path, and the supplier contracts are all already paid for, updated incrementally, with nothing requiring engineering from scratch. So, the SV-7GX gets to spend the savings elsewhere. Everything wrapped around the engine is new. Ride-by-wire throttle, three power modes, and a bidirectional quickshifter, none of which existed on this platform before. Plus, it now runs a five-mode traction control system that replaces the three-mode setup the V-Strom 650 has run for years, thanks to the ride-by-wire tech. A 4.2-inch color TFT display runs Suzuki's Ride Connect+ smartphone connectivity, with a USB-C port to keep a phone charged. Despite the contemporary bodywork, the tech isn’t exotic on its own, as rivals running newer, pricier engines have offered ride-by-wire and quickshifters for years. What's notable is that Suzuki plastered the tech on an engine that's possibly older than some of its buyers. The same logic that kept the engine unchanged carries into the chassis as well. Suzuki wrapped the value-focused SV-7GX around the SV650's tubular steel trellis frame, running a 41mm fork with no adjustment beyond what the rear shock offers through seven steps of preload. Four-piston calipers bite twin 290mm discs up front, with a single 240mm disc doing braking work out back. Wheels are 17-inch cast aluminum wrapped in Pirelli Angel GT II rubber that rounds up the running gear. Ergonomically, the SV-7GX splits the difference between its two donor bikes. The rider’s triangle is closer to the upright stance of the V-Strom 650, albeit being sportier. A seat height of 31.3 inches and curb weight of 465 pounds make it approachable for a rider stepping up or getting their first bike. Cruise control doesn't make the cut here, and is the clearest sign of where Suzuki drew the line for pricier tech inclusion. The Kawasaki Versys 650 LT ABS costs $10,399, and the extra $1,800 buys advantages like a 5.5-gallon tank for more range and a fork adjustable for both rebound and preload. But it’s heavier at 482.9 pounds, and its 649cc parallel-twin makes less power than the SV-7GX’s more character-rich V-twin. Elsewhere, the Triumph Tiger Sport 660 is the one with more power from its 659cc inline-triple. But it’s tech-laden with a six-axis IMU-linked cornering ABS and standard cruise control. It’s also a bike that is still priced competitively at $10,445, but that’s nearly a solid $2,000 more than the SV-7GX. The Honda NC750X DCT brings an automatic gearbox into the mix, and adds a 23-liter storage compartment in place of a conventionally placed fuel tank. At $9,499, it's the closest rival on price, but it's also the heaviest of the four here at 497 pounds. Cost is the foremost factor here in favor of the SV-7GX, and all three rivals cost more. Yet, only the SV-7GX bundles ride-by-wire, a bidirectional quickshifter, and five-mode traction control into its $8,599 sticker price. That not only makes it a smart build by Suzuki, but possibly the smartest motorcycle buy of the year in this class. We want to hear from you. title: Fulham v Chelsea: Key stats and talking points - BBC
content: Week one of the 2026-27 Premier League season signals the start of a new era for London rivals Fulham and Chelsea. They meet on Monday night (20:00 BST) at Craven Cottage. The home side have a new coach in the dugout for the first time in five years. Marco Silva moved on at the end of last season following the expiration of his contract, and Fulham made the bold choice to appoint former Real Madrid boss Alvaro Arbeloa as his replacement. As for Chelsea, after a tumultuous 2025-26 season in which they had three different head coaches, they have opted for Xabi Alonso – another former Real Madrid boss – to steady the ship and take the team forward. For Alonso and Arbeloa, this season will be about shaking off challenging respective campaigns in the Spanish capital. The former took charge of Los Blancos at the start last season and was replaced by his former Liverpool team-mate after being sacked in January. Arbeloa also found the Madrid squad too tricky to tame and was given his marching orders at the end of the season. A fresh start should do both of them good in theory. Arbeloa has sought to bring some gems from the Bernabeu with him to west London, though, with Gonzalo Garcia and Cesar Palacios signing from Real Madrid. They could help Arbeloa make an early imprint on a squad that was forged in Silva's image over five years. A fast start is something that has eluded the Cottagers in recent seasons too, as they have won just one of their past six Premier League openers. After being appointed in May, Alonso has had plenty of time to put together his plan for the new campaign. While Chelsea have spent big again, there has been a shift in their transfer strategy. Across the previous seven transfer windows, the Blues have signed 30 players at an average age of 20.5; this summer, they have added eight first-team players with an average age of 25.6. The arrivals of 35-year-old Danny Welbeck and 36-year-old Jordan Henderson would indicate that Alonso feels some experience is essential in what remains a young squad. They will both be keen to offer something on the pitch too, though. Welbeck, in particular, was fantastic for Brighton last season and netted 13 times in the Premier League. This year will be a significant one for the former Manchester United and Arsenal man. Welbeck is set to feature in his 19th Premier League season, playing at least once in every campaign since and including 2008-09. This will be the joint-most seasons played by any striker in the competition's history, equalling Jermain Defoe (19) and overtaking Peter Crouch (18). Welbeck and the rest of the new acquisitions will be key in uplifting the Chelsea squad after the wheels fell off last season in spectacular fashion. From the start of March, the Blues lost a whopping eight Premier League matches, which was the most of any team in the division. title: These Are The V-Twin Engines That Power Arch Motorcycles - Jalopnik
content: You hear that? It's the unmistakable report of a V-Twin, the iconic engine configuration you'll find in damn near every Milwaukee-built motorcycle since Harley-Davidson's switch to V-Twins in the early 1900s (and the headache that came along with doubling an H-D's number of cylinders). Today, well over a century after the V-Twin started powering Harley-Davidson and Indian motorcycles, you can find the popular configuration in everything from big lazy domestic cruisers to metric bikes. However, Harley-Davidson and Indian Motorcycles aren't the only names in American-made motorcycles anymore, especially when it comes to high-dollar performance cruisers. If you've got the money to make it happen, you can buy a bike from California-based Arch Motorcycles. The brand deals in bespoke motorcycle offerings, and, though customizable, they feature a familiar presence in the cruiser segment: the V-Twin. Specifically, Arch-fiddled S&S V-Twin engines power the brand's bikes. Don't think of the carbureted overhead-valve S&S mill in your buddy's chopper, though. Every Arch motorcycle features a fuel-injected big twin with a downdraft intake system. The brand's racing aspirations, however, might change things. Some celebrities diversify and pin their names to liquor, clothing, and even mobile phone brands (looking at you, Ryan Reynolds). Others, like none other than Keanu Reeves, would rather spend time building bikes that "challenge the perception of what an American motorcycle could be." Yes, that Keanu Reeves. The same guy who played Neo in "The Matrix" and lovable nitwit Ted in the "Bill and Ted" movie franchise. Along with co-founder and custom bike builder Gard Hollinger, the actor launched Arch Motorcycles back in 2011. The Arch KRGT-1 was the brand's first performance cruiser model, and it features, you guessed it, an Arch/S&S V-Twin engine. It's a 124 cubic-inch twin, seven cubes more than the displacement you'd find in a comparable, albeit much more affordable and less unique, performance cruiser from the Bar & Shield, such as the Low Rider S. Unlike the Milwaukee-Eight V-Twin in the Low Rider S, the Arch/S&S twin features a downdraft intake system, slimming things down by eliminating the more typical side-draft layout. In the KRGT-1 and the race-inspired, more aggressive Arch 1s, the Arch/S&S T124 45-degree twin produces 115.3 pound-feet of torque at the rear wheel. The rarer-than-unicorn-tears Arch Method143 packs an even stouter S&S mill. The Method143's engine displaces 2,343 cubic centimeters (143 cubic inches). Arch says that big-boy twin is good for 151 pound-feet of smile-inducing twist. Better budget for rear tires in addition to the Method143's likely sweltering cost. An Arch/S&S engine won't forever be the only mill you find in one of the brand's creations. Keanu Reeves and Gard Hollinger are building the future of Arch Motorcycles, and, spoiler alert, it's got a different engine at its core. It's the company's new 2s-R Super Hooligan bike. With riders Corey Alexander and Jeremy McWilliams aboard, Arch hopes to flex its new engine: a 119-cubic-inch twin developed in partnership with Switzerland's Suter Industries. Still, S&S engines are a popular option for cruiser fans and custom bike builders. Outside of powering production Arch motorcycles, S&S builds and sells entire assembled V-Twin engines, ranging from modern interpretations of the classic Knucklehead twin to cammed replacements for the current Milwaukee-Eight V-Twin you'd see in Harley-Davidson cruisers and tourers, like the ever-popular Street Glide and Road Glide. For now, a lumpy, beating S&S heart is what you'll find in your bike when you build a bespoke motorcycle with Arch. After all, what's more American in motorcycling than an air-cooled V-Twin? That's exactly what Arch says it set out to do with its pricey, adrenaline-summoning, and bespoke motorcycles.

New Orleans would turn the ball over on downs during their next series leading to another Bennett TD run. title: 3 things learned - sort of - from Colts v. Falcons preseason game - Yahoo Sports
content: Following the Indianapolis Colts' performance from Week 2 of the preseason, what did we learn about this team? With battles for playing time and roster spots up for grabs this time of the year, one would hope to come out of each preseason game with some added clarity. That only sort of happened this week for the Colts. Here is what we think we learned, or at least observed. What we can say right now is that Akeem Davis-Gaither will be one of the starters. He has not played in either preseason game. But who will be lining up next to him this season remains to be seen. Against Atlanta, the Colts relied on a heavy rotation, likely searching for answers. Jaylon Carlies and Austin Ajiake were the first two on the field, followed by rookies CJ Allen and Bryce Boettcher. The two duos then alternated series. Each linebacker brings something different to the defense. Carlies, a former safety, adds a coverage presence. Boettcher has impressed playing downhill and as a blitzer, while Allen's well-rounded skill set allows him to impact the game in a variety of ways. Given how the last week of practices has gone, it may be Carlies who is the favorite right now to start next to Davis-Gaither. That said, Lou Anarumo hasn't ruled out utilizing a rotation in-season, with the matchups and in-game situations dictating who is on the field. The depth of this unit has been a question all offseason, and through two preseason games, it still remains to be seen whether or not the Colts have enough pass rush juice behind Laiatu Latu. Caden Curry popped in the preseason opener, but it was a quiet week for Jaylahn Tuimoloau and Micheal Clemons. This week, no Colts' pass rusher was able to consistently get after the quarterback. According to ESPN, the Colts finished with one sack and only one quarterback hit, both of which came later in the game. Not surprisingly, without steady pressure, the Atlanta quarterbacks were quite efficient passing the ball. Riley Leonard again underwhelmed. Starting for the Colts in this game, Leonard completed just 7-of-14 passes for 62 yards, and 39 of those total yards came on a wide-open completion to Coleman Owen. Leonard averaged only 4.4 yards per pass attempt. He did not have an interception but did fumble a snap that he was able to recover. In two preseason games, Leonard has struggled to get into any sort of rhythm. Anthony Richardson didn't fare any better in the passing game, completing 3-of-9 passes, but his ability to extend plays when under pressure did help keep drives alive. His presence under center adds a different element to the Colts' offense for defenses to contend with. Both quarterbacks had to deal with shaky offensive line play, and it looked like the wide receivers struggled to create separation. title: Actor Michael Wright, Star of ‘The Five Heartbeats’ and ‘V,’ Dies at 70 - Variety
content:
Michael Wright, an actor known for his roles in “The Five Heartbeats,” “Streamers,” “The Principal” and “V,” has died, according to a statement from his family. He was 70. His wife, Susan Wright, announced his death in a post shared Friday evening on Instagram. “It is with profound sadness and an unimaginable heaviness in my heart that I share the passing of my beloved husband, Michael Wright,” her statement read. Wright’s family said he died in Los Angeles on Wednesday, Aug. 19, after suffering heart failure coupled with complications of degenerative neurological disease Marchiafava-Bignami, according to a statement provided to TMZ. Wright was born on April 30, 1956, in New York City. He appeared in more than 50 movies and TV shows, including the films “The Five Heartbeats,” Robert Altman’s Vietnam drama “Streamers,” “Sugar Hill” and “The Wanderers.” His TV credits include the 1980s sci-fi series “V” and HBO’s “Oz.” In the Robert Townsend-directed 1991 musical film “The Five Heartbeats,” about a fictional Motown group, Wright played the band’s charismatic lead vocalist, Eddie King Jr., whose alcohol and drug addiction forces him to leave the Heartbeats. “Michael was a husband, a father (Manon Wright, Byron Barr, Brittney Briggs, Brianna Barr, Sir Barr, a grandfather (Yoko), loved one, a friend, and an extraordinary artist whose work touched generations,” Susan’s statement said. “Many knew and loved him through ‘The Five Heartbeats,’ ‘The Wanderers,’ ‘V,’ ‘The Principal,’ ‘Streamers,’ and the many other characters he brought to life throughout his remarkable career. His talent, presence, and contributions to film and television will live on, but to those of us who loved him personally, he was so much more than the roles the world knew him for.” Her statement continued, “Our family is grieving an enormous and deeply personal loss. We understand how much Michael meant to so many people, and we are grateful for the love, prayers, memories, and condolences already being shared. … In the coming days, when we are ready, we will share additional information regarding Michael’s life, legacy, and how we intend to honor and celebrate him.” Susan concluded, “Michael, your work will live forever, but your love will live even longer in the hearts of those who knew you best. Rest peacefully, my love. You will be missed beyond words.” In a 2021 interview with Sheen Magazine, Wright said, “The greatest sin an actor can commit is to fail to be interesting. I always try to make my characters interesting. I want you to be riveted and wonder what’s going on behind my eyes.” Wright also said there wasn’t anything in his life he would do over: “I’ve done everything I have wanted to do. I’ve been everywhere, I speak five different languages. I have seen the world; I love my experiences.” 3 Comments Comments are moderated. title: UND Law Professor Carolyn V. Williams Receives 2026 Outstanding Service Award - University of North Dakota (UND)
content: Updates from the University of North Dakota School of Law. University of North Dakota School of Law Professor Carolyn V. Williams has received the 2026 Outstanding Service Award from the Association of Legal Writing Directors (ALWD). The ALWD Board of Directors voted unanimously to recognize Williams for her work as author of the eighth edition of the ALWD Guide to Legal Citation. In announcing the award, the Board highlighted not only the extensive work involved in revising the Guide, but also Williams’s efforts to engage the legal writing community in developing new rules addressing the use and citation of generative artificial intelligence. The Board praised Williams for developing “common-sense and functional AI rules” and for her work promoting the Guide as a citation resource for law students, professors, lawyers, and judges. ALWD is a national professional organization dedicated to advancing legal writing and supporting legal writing professionals as teachers, scholars, and leaders. Among its major initiatives, ALWD publishes the ALWD Guide to Legal Citation, a nationally used legal citation manual designed to make citation clear, accessible, and practical for students and practicing lawyers alike. The Guide also plays an important role in supporting ALWD’s broader mission, including by helping to fund a range of programs and initiatives that support legal writing faculty in developing innovative teaching materials and pursuing scholarly projects. Williams authored both the seventh and eighth editions of the Guide. The newly released eighth edition includes substantial updates reflecting changes in legal research and practice, including a new rule addressing when and how lawyers and legal scholars should acknowledge or cite the use of generative AI. Following completion of the eighth edition, Williams was also hired as a consultant by LexisNexis to revise and rewrite its Interactive Citation Workshop exercises for the ALWD Guide, ensuring that the online exercises used by law students and legal writing professors align with the eighth edition’s updated rules and citation standards. Williams will be formally recognized for the Outstanding Service Award at ALWD’s 2027 Biennial Conference. title: DC’s ‘People v. Gorilla Grodd’ Mockumentary Series Set at HBO Max, Skyler Gisondo and Jimmy Tatro to Star - Variety
content:
"American Vandal" creators Tony Yacenda and Dan Perrault will serve as showrunners HBO Max is officially moving forward with their DC Studios mockumentary series, now titled “The People v. Gorilla Grodd.” The show was first reported to be in the works in November 2025. As reported at the time, Skyler Gisondo will reprise the role of Jimmy Olsen, whom he first played in the 2025 “Superman” movie. Jimmy Tatro is officially set to play Gorilla Grodd. HBO Max has given the show an eight-episode order. The logline for the show states, “A superintelligent ape (Tatro) is convicted of murdering his father, the King of Gorilla City. In an eight-part ‘true’ crime docuseries, the Daily Planet’s Jimmy Olsen (Gisondo) reopens the case, investigating whether Gorilla Grodd was wrongly convicted in one of Metropolis’ most famous murder trials.” Along with Gisondo and Tatro, the series will also star “Superman” actors Beck Bennett as Steve Lombard, Mikaela Hoover as Cat Grant, and Wendell Pierce as Perry White. Additional cast members include Mary Holland, Eduardo Franco, Arian Moayed, Andrew Leeds, and Tim Baltz. Tony Yacenda and Dan Perrault will serve as writers, executive producers, and showrunners on the series, with Perrault also set as part of the show’s cast. Yacenda will direct all eight episodes. James Gunn and Peter Safran also executive produce. DC Studios and Warner Bros. Television will produce. “We’re excited by the challenge of creating a series that feels less like an entry into the DCU and more like an artifact from it,” Yacenda and Perrault said. “A Daily Planet original documentary made for the people of Metropolis. We hope it’ll appeal to fans of the comics, comedy and true crime. And while we can’t speak for audiences here yet, we already know it’s a huge hit in Metropolis. They love this series.” Yacenda and Perrault are no strangers to the world of mockumentary series. The duo famously created the critically-acclaimed Netflix show “American Vandal,” which spoofed the true crime genre. The show aired for two seasons at the streamer and won a Peabody Award for its first season in addition to being nominated for an Emmy for best writing for a comedy series. Tatro and Franco both starred in the show’s first season. Yacenda and Perrault then went on to create the Paramount+ mockumentary series “Players,” which was set in the world of eSports. They previously spoofed the sports world on projects like a parody of ESPN’s “30 for 30” series about the events of “Rocky IV” and “Angels in the Outfield” for CollegeHumor. “We are thrilled to be working with Tony and Dan, alongside James, Peter, the entire DC team and our colleagues at WBTV, to bring these iconic DCU characters to HBO Max in a new and unexpected way,” said Amy Gravitt, executive vice president of HBO Programming and ead of HBO & HBO Max comedy series. “We already know Skyler Gisondo is pitch-perfect as Jimmy Olsen and we can’t wait for fans to experience Jimmy Tatro’s captivating and hilarious portrayal of Grodd.” Gunn and Safran added, “Between Skyler’s wonderful performance and the fantastic chemistry of the Daily Planet cast, we knew coming out of ‘Superman’ that this would be a fun world to explore. We’re excited to work with the brilliant Dan Perrault and Tony Yacenda to take the audience down some of the darker and funnier streets and alleyways of the DCU as Jimmy spotlights the Metropolis criminal justice system for his docuseries.” Gisondo is repped by UTA, Untitled Entertainment and Jackoway Austen. Tatro is repped by Brillstein Entertainment, UTA, Toczek Suddleson Law Group LLP and Luna Public Relations. Bennett is repped by UTA and Myman Greenspan. Hoover is repped by Buchwald, Untitled Entertainment, Brecheen Feldman Breimer Silver Thompson, and Birch Public Relations. Pierce is repped by Paradigm. Holland is repped by Atlas Artists, Paradigm Talent Agency, and Ziffren Brittenham. Franco is repped by Mosaic, UTA & Kovert Creative. Moayed is repped by UTA and Kipperman Management. Perrault is repped by Brillstein, UTA, and Narrative. Leeds is repped by Gersh, Perennial Entertainment, and Felker Toczek Suddleson McGinnis Ryan LLP. Baltz is repped by repped by El Centro Entertainment, Gersh, and Lichter-Grossman. News of the series order comes less than a week after the premiere of “Lanterns,” another DC Studios show about Green Lanterns John Stewart and Hal Jordan. It was reported last week that two DC live-action projects — an Amanda Waller series and a “Wonder Woman” prequel set on Themyscira — are no longer in development. 3 Comments Comments are moderated. (Cadillac/TNS) The 2026 Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing offers a 6.2-liter V8 producing 668 horsepower and 659 pound-feet of torque. (Cadillac/TNS) The luxury sedan is supposed to be extinct. The industry has held the memorial service, lowered the casket, and handed out little sandwiches to the mourners. Thankfully for everyone who enjoys driving, Cadillac forgot to attend. Instead, it built the CT5-V Blackwing: a four-door luxury sedan with the temperament of a disgruntled executive who has discovered that the company wellness seminar is actually about feelings. This is not a vehicle designed by people who believe the automotive future is a silent pod carrying commuters between approved lifestyle zones. The Blackwing is built around an old-fashioned idea that a car should occasionally make you grin like an idiot. It has a supercharged V-8, available manual transmission, and enough performance capability to make you question whether the engineers were given a budget or simply left unsupervised. It starts with Cadillac’s CT5 midsize sedan, a vehicle that looks more like an old Nissan than a new Cadillac. Then it adds the usual go-fast dross attached to modern-day sports sedans. But the overall effect plays into the CT5’s adrenaline-fueled style, signaling its seriousness as a nuclear track weapon. Certainly, GM has loaded it with its best performance goodies. The test car was fitted with the $18,000 Precision Package, a collection of hardware and software upgrades aimed squarely at extracting maximum performance on the track. The package adds stiffer front springs, revised bushings, a larger front stabilizer bar, and unique front steering knuckles and rear toe links to achieve a more aggressive track-focused alignment. Stopping power comes courtesy of Brembo carbon-ceramic brakes, which deliver enormous bite while resisting fade during repeated high-speed track sessions. Their job is made easier by a set of ultra-high-performance Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2 R tires, essentially racing rubber with just enough street manners to avoid requiring its own trailer. The package also includes recalibrated software systems, with retuned MagneRide dampers, steering, the electronic limited-slip differential (eLSD), and Performance Traction Management (PTM) all optimized to work with the sharper suspension setup and increased tire grip. The result is a CT5-V Blackwing that feels less like a fast luxury sedan and more like a road-legal track weapon that happens to have a back seat. At the heart of the Blackwing is a supercharged 6.2-liter V-8 producing 668 horsepower and 659 pound-feet of torque. It’s large, powerful, and gloriously out of step with the modern obsession with making every object behave like a sensible appliance. A washing machine does not need character. A car with a V-8 and an available manual gearbox does. And that gearbox matters. In an age where many cars are trying to remove the driver from the driving experience, preferably while adding another touchscreen, Cadillac hands you the controls and has you participate. It’s inconvenient, occasionally awkward, and vastly more rewarding than clicking a button and waiting for the car to decide you have earned acceleration privileges. Power goes to the rear wheels, and buyers can choose a 10-speed automatic if they wish. The manual is the enthusiast’s choice, which is another way of saying it’s the choice made by people who enjoy adding unnecessary effort to something a computer could technically do faster. These are also the people who still own mechanical watches, and get up to switch the TV channel. The Blackwing’s acceleration is dramatic, with 60 mph coming in 3.4 seconds with the automatic, 3.6 seconds with the manual. But the experience is more impressive than the stopwatch. The engine does not simply produce power; it announces its availability. The throttle response, the exhaust note, and the sensation of the rear tires negotiating with physics all combine into something that feels increasingly rare: a car with a fun personality. The chassis is equally serious. The CT5-V Blackwing uses Cadillac’s performance expertise to deliver sharp handling, strong braking capability, and a level of composure that allows the car to transition from comfortable highway cruiser to enthusiastic back-road weapon without requiring a personality transplant from the driver. That dual nature is the Blackwing’s greatest trick. It can behave like a premium sedan when you need to pretend that you’re a responsible adult. Then, with a conveniently empty stretch of road, it can remind you that the automotive engineers involved clearly had some unresolved issues with moderation. The remarkable thing is that the Blackwing is not merely a fast sedan wearing a luxury badge. It’s a genuinely sophisticated machine that can carry you through daily life without making you feel like you have purchased a very expensive punishment device. Inside, the Blackwing provides the expected luxury appointments and technology. Pop for the $8,090 semi-aniline leather seats with custom quilting and carbon fiber seatbacks and you’ll be treated to seriously sporty, and form thrones that provide all-day comfort and support without feeling punishing. Overall, it feels as posh as expected, despite a notoriously cheap lower door trim panel. Yet the main attraction is not the number of screens, electronic conveniences. Or its new for 2026 Performance Data Recorder. The highlight is the fact that Cadillac still built a car where the driver is part of the process rather than a passenger supervising the software. There are compromises. Fuel economy is not the Blackwing’s hobby. Rear-seat space is useful but not limousine-like. And despite its impressive capability, the sedan market is shrinking, meaning this car exists in a category that has been abandoned by many manufacturers in favor of taller vehicles that make everyone feel like they are commanding a small apartment building. But that is precisely why the CT5-V Blackwing matters. It’s not practical in the way a crossover is practical. It’s not efficient in the way an electric vehicle is efficient. It is not anonymous in the way so many modern luxury cars have become. It’s a machine built around the radical idea that driving should be entertaining. title: 2026 Honda CR-V Hybrid vs. Hyundai Tucson Hybrid: Which Is the Better Buy? - GreenCars
content: ⚙️ Output: The CR-V Hybrid makes 204 horsepower, while the Tucson Hybrid makes 231 horsepower 🚗 Drivetrain: Both the CR-V Hybrid and Tucson Hybrid offer front- or all-wheel drive ⛽ Fuel Economy (EPA estimated): The CR-V Hybrid gets up to 40 mpg combined, while the Tucson Hybrid gets up to 38 mpg combined 🖥️ Tech: The CR-V Hybrid gets a 9.0-inch touchscreen, while the Tucson Hybrid gets a 12.3-inch touchscreen 🧳 Cargo: The CR-V Hybrid holds 36.3 cu ft behind the second row, while the Tucson Hybrid holds 41.2 cu ft 💰MSRP: The CR-V Hybrid starts at an MSRP of $37,080, while the Tucson Hybrid starts at an MSRP of $32,950 The small SUV market typically isn’t the most exciting segment to talk about, but it's the one Americans are most likely to gravitate toward. These smaller utilities account for 19 percent of the market so far in 2026, with 37 percent more sales than full-size pickups. In 2025, Honda sold more than 200,000 CR-V Hybrids, making it one of the bestselling small hybrid SUVs on the market. The Hyundai Tucson Hybrid’s sales figures are quite a bit smaller than that, but they've grown considerably over the past few years. Honda offers the CR-V in both hybrid and nonhybrid powertrains, while Hyundai adds a plug-in variant to the Tucson lineup. The Honda CR-V Hybrid's last redesign was in 2023. It’s not an old design, but with so many sales, it’s a pretty familiar sight almost anywhere you go. Honda really wants to emphasize the “s” in SUV, as all four of its hybrid trim levels tout “sport” in one way or another. All jokes aside, it’s a stylish vehicle with a design that leans more toward classic and timeless than trendy and bold. For a deeper look at Honda’s comfort, efficiency, and everyday driving experience, see how the top-spec CR-V Hybrid performs in a full road test ➜ The Tucson Hybrid’s design is quite different and leans toward the latter of that description. It takes on a rounded shape, a large front grille, and sharp lines and dimensional carvings down the side of the vehicle. It's without a doubt sportier than its predecessor, but its design might be a little bold for some drivers. These two small hybrid SUVs are pretty competitive in size. You’ll only find an inch of difference or less between most of their measurements. The only notable gap comes in the cargo hold, where the Tucson Hybrid has slightly more space than the CR-V Hybrid. So if you’re packing a double stroller or you're a regular visitor to your local big box store, you might find the Tucson Hybrid a bit more flexible. Both vehicles come standard with cloth upholstery, dual climate controls, USB-C charging ports, and wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto. The Tucson Hybrid’s 12.3-inch touchscreen dwarfs the Honda’s 9.0-inch. Heated front seats, a power moonroof, and a power driver’s seat are standard on the CR-V Hybrid but are upgrades on the Tucson Hybrid. Both can be had with leather upholstery, a wireless charging pad, a Bose premium sound system, a heated steering wheel, a power liftgate, and driver's seat memory settings. If ventilated front seats or heated rear seats are on your must-have list, you won’t find them on the CR-V Hybrid’s list of available features. The Tucson Hybrid offers those, plus some other niceties like a 12.3-inch digital instrument cluster and a 12-inch head-up display. The Honda also offers an upgraded 10.2-inch digital instrument cluster, but overall, its list of available features is shorter than what’s offered in the Hyundai. As far as safety suites go, both have a standard driver-assist suite that includes adaptive cruise control, blind-spot monitoring, automatic emergency braking, lane-keeping assist, lane-following assist, driver-attention warning, rear-occupant alert, and rear cross-traffic alert. The Tucson Hybrid’s standard suite also includes safe-exit assist, while the CR-V Hybrid's includes traffic-sign recognition. The Tucson Hybrid can be had with forward-attention warning, a blind-spot view monitor, navigation-based cruise control, parking collision-avoidance assist, parking sensors, remote smart parking assist, a surround-view monitor, highway-driving assist, and an advanced rear-occupant alert with an in-cabin radar sensor that can detect children or animals accidentally left in the vehicle — though don’t expect that last one to stick around, since Hyundai has already dropped it from 2027 models. Parking sensors are available on upper CR-V Hybrid trims. Both the CR-V Hybrid and Tucson Hybrid offer a choice between front- and all-wheel drive. On fuel economy, the CR-V Hybrid offers the most impressive figures, earning up to 43 mpg in city driving and 40 mpg combined for the front-drive model. The best the Tucson Hybrid can manage is 38 mpg combined. If saving money at the pump is your top priority, the Honda wins all day long. A two-mpg headline difference does not always translate directly to the same real-world fuel savings, so see what EPA city, highway, and combined fuel-economy ratings actually mean ➜ When it comes to price, the Hyundai Tucson Hybrid beats the Honda CR-V Hybrid. Every trim except its top level is more affordable than the least expensive CR-V Hybrid. Both models top out in the lower $40,000s, but if features matter more to you than fuel economy, the Tucson Hybrid is your best bet. Both of these vehicles are pleasant to drive, with comfortable ride quality and handling that's capable, if not sports-car-like. However, the driving experience differs quite a bit due to their different hybrid architectures. The Honda's hybrid system is configured to run mostly as a series hybrid and packs nearly three times the electric motor output of the Tucson Hybrid's. During most driving, only the electric motor drives the wheels, with the engine only turning a generator to provide electricity. A clutch engages to send some engine power to the wheels at highway speeds. The result is a quiet overall ride that feels more like driving an EV. The Hyundai's hybrid system uses a smaller motor sandwiched between the engine and a conventional six-speed automatic transmission. That makes it feel much more like a traditional gas-only vehicle, albeit generally quieter. It doesn’t have the overall refinement of the Honda, however. For more time behind the wheel of Hyundai’s turbo-hybrid setup, see how the Tucson Hybrid balances power, refinement, space, and family usability ➜ Either way, you get a surprisingly roomy crossover that delivers excellent fuel efficiency and a long feature list. The Hyundai feels a bit more modern inside, with larger screens and a bolder exterior design, while the Honda goes a bit more traditional all around. Functionality, though, is pretty similar between the two. Choosing between the CR-V Hybrid and Tucson Hybrid really comes down to personal preference. If you want a design that stands out from the crowd, the Tucson Hybrid is absolutely your winner. The front-wheel-drive CR-V Hybrid will yield you a couple of extra mpg, but those fuel savings aren’t quite enough to overcome the price gap of over $3,000 more upfront on base trims. If you want the most EV-like driving experience without a plug, get the CR-V Hybrid. title: VMAN 57: Belmont Cameli Is In Demand - V Magazine
content: After nearly a decade in the industry, the breakout Off Campus star is turning heads and opening doors After nearly a decade in the industry, the breakout Off Campus star is turning heads and opening doors When Belmont Cameli stepped into the skates of Off Campus’s Garrett Graham, he relied on Elle Kennedy’s novel of the same name more as guidance than scripture. He swapped literary Garrett’s penchant for Led Zeppelin with Arcade Fire (“That’s my version of the taste Garrett has,” he says), softening the literary character’s boisterous edges, concocting an all-too-easy-to-love student athlete with a true lived-in warmth. In his conversation with Grammy Award-winning singer-songwriter Laufey, it becomes increasingly clear what pumps the blood through Garrett’s beating heart: Cameli himself. Many fans first met the charismatic actor in 2020’s Saved by the Bell remake, but lacing up skates for Prime Video this year really plugged him into fancams and TikTok FYPs (including Laufey’s) globally. Amid his shooting schedule for Off Campus’s hotly awaited second season, Cameli sat down with Laufey to chat about Joshua Tree, ballet, and the necessity of leaning into fear. LAUFEY: I feel like I’ve been watching your star rise in the past few months, and it’s always so exciting to see artists, especially of different mediums, have their moment. And this is so, so deserved. BELMONT CAMELI: Yeah, for me too, watching you come up was probably the same feeling. L: I’m so excited to talk to you, because we met before. I feel like I ran into you one time at a party or something, or I feel like you were with your mom. BC: I think we ran into each other at the Melrose Flea or like the Silver Lake Flea—at a flea market. L: That does check out. So are you still living in LA? BC: Not really. I was in Laurel Canyon for a while, and then I moved out last fall, and now I don’t really have a lease anywhere. I’ve just been kind of bouncing around, but I spend the summers here in Vancouver, which is nice. L: You’ve been filming [Off Campus] in Vancouver, right? BC: Yeah, so we’re here for five months during the summers, and then I just kind of bounce around—mostly New York and LA—when I’m not working. L: Where do you go when you want to unwind? I definitely have that one place that I go to, and I just want to reset and forget about the industry. BC: Home definitely does that for me. When I’m in LA, it’s Joshua Tree. I usually make a point to go out there a couple of times a year with a small group of friends. I like to get, like, a shitty Airbnb, ideally with a bunch of desert garbage kind of around because that’s a theme out there. That’s my retreat, and then I also go to Mount Baldy, which is an hour east of L.A. It’s a really quite high summit, and there’s this little lodge, Mount Baldy Lodge, that’s kind of trapped in the ’70s, and it’s really a great drive. It’s a great hike, and it’s just a nice place to get away. L: I hear from a lot of people that when they go to Joshua Treats, it’s a very spiritual experience. Do you feel a connection with a higher power there? I don’t know. BC: There’s something about the sound of the desert. It’s so quiet out there, and the echo is so pronounced. You can have a conversation in a normal normal talking volume with somebody who’s super far away. Sound just travels differently in the desert. I’ve certainly had some spiritual experiences out there. L: I think especially when you’re an artist, having that go-to where you know you can connect to something beyond is very [important]. It’s a little woo woo, but I kind of love it. So, my next question. You are truly the man of the moment right now, and I feel like all my friends are talking about you, and you’re all over my FYP and everything. BC: I think for me, it’s weird to say that I feel cut out for it because it’s certainly been weird and hard in certain cases, just because of this sudden nature of it. It’s not that I was ever hoping to be famous, but I always wanted to have success in this career and understood that that would be a facet or symptom of the work. The biggest thing that’s changed for me has been that the number on the app on my phone has gone up. You know what I mean? But my reality is that the things I can see with my eyes are all exactly the same. I’ve always been extremely wary to digest that type of hype. It’s been a bit of an adjustment. I think the biggest thing I’ve noticed is—like, I was in New York last weekend, and one of my favorite things to do is just walk all day long, go get 15,000 steps, and that was a little more challenging. Honestly, I had a kind of sad moment resigning to that anonymity after a day spent out in New York of like, ‘Oh man, I can’t just enjoy the solitude of being in a big world as much as I used to.’ But people are always really nice; they enjoy the thing that I’ve worked really hard on. So that’s really sweet. I still feel very much like the same person, and the best part is now I’ll hopefully have some more opportunities on the other side of this, which is what I care about: the work. L: It seems like you have a healthy outlook on it and a good head on your shoulders. BC: I’m not on the internet like that, which is super helpful. BC: It’s terrible. I think when people say something nice, if that makes you feel good, then people have this same power to make you feel bad when they say something mean and rude. So I try not to ingest either. L: What I’ve been thinking a lot about this year is how I’ve done all these tours and written this music, and I know what it’s like to do these things, so I want to try things that scare me a little bit. I was like, ‘Should I jump out of a plane?’ But then I was like, ‘I really don’t want to jump out of a plane.’ Does anything scare you? BC: Oh my god, all the time. But that’s kind of my favorite. A lot of the greatest growth I’ve achieved as a person and an artist has been on the other side of things that scared me the most. My instrument is my brain and my body. That’s what I had to continually fine-tune, and that’s a never-ending process. The more life experience I have, the more I have to pull from, and having a range of experiences is really important. So I never neglect things that scare me. Those are the most essential parts of life. When I can apply those to the work, that’s where the fulfillment comes from. But yeah, I’ve done a lot of things that scare me—leaving school in the first place to become an actor was kind of horrifying. But it’s no fun to do something that isn’t challenging. L: I heard that on top of being an actor, you are also a filmmaker, and that’s something you want to be a part of your journey. What inspires you? What kind of stories do you want to tell? BC: There’s a lot I want to do right now. I’m focused on building out my body of work as an actor, but I can’t wait to direct. When I write, comedy flows from me the most naturally, so I look forward to working on comedy. I’ve always been a big fan of both blockbuster comedies and niche, offbeat comedies. L: There hasn’t been enough of that in the past couple of years. So you’ll bring that back. BC: I completely agree. I mean, that was the heartbeat of my fan experience as a kid, all these big Steve Carell, Will Ferrell, and Jim Carrey [movies]. I agree there could and should be more of them. I love comedy. It’s my favorite. I grew up as a student of Robin Williams, David Letterman, and these comedy legends. Norm Macdonald was one of my favorite standups. These people I revere. I also really want to write a drama about ballet because my sister was a ballerina, and I’ve always been appreciative of that art form as an audience member. It would be a great challenge athletically. I’ve gotten to play different types of athletes now, and I think it would be really fulfilling. The things they do in their movement and as athletes are fascinating. The life of a ballerina is usually pretty unglamorous and very difficult, so that’s a story I would love to tell someday. We’ll see. L: That’s super cool. If you need someone to score it or work on music, you know exactly who to call now. This cover story appears in the pages of VMAN 57: now available for purchase! title: Hyundai Ioniq V starts pre-sales in China from $17,700 - CnEVPost
content: Beijing Hyundai, Hyundai Motor's joint venture in China, opened pre-sales for the Ioniq V at the 2026 Chengdu Auto Show, which kicked off on Friday, advancing the automaker's product offensive in the world's largest electric vehicle market. The Ioniq V is available in 3 variants, with pre-sales prices ranging from 119,900 yuan ($17,680) to 139,900 yuan, and is scheduled to officially launch in September. The 540 Max is priced at 119,900 yuan, the 540 Max+ at 129,900 yuan, and the 650 Max+ at 139,900 yuan. All 3 variants currently available for pre-sales are battery electric vehicles, offering a CLTC range of up to 650 km and supporting an 800-volt high-voltage fast-charging system. Previous information has indicated that the Ioniq V lineup may also add an extended-range electric vehicle (EREV) version in the future. The Ioniq V is the first production model from Hyundai's Ioniq brand in China and the production version of the Venus Concept unveiled at the Beijing Auto Show in April. The mid-size sedan was led throughout its development by Hyundai's China design center and tailored for Chinese consumers. Hyundai also plans to offer the model in overseas markets. The vehicle measures 4,900 mm in length, 1,890 mm in width and 1,470 mm in height, with a wheelbase of 2,900 mm. It features a fastback profile and frameless doors. The Ioniq V is based on Hyundai's E-GMP (Electric Global Modular Platform) and offers single-motor versions with maximum outputs of 140 kW and 168 kW. Its batteries are supplied by CATL (HKEX: 3750), using lithium iron phosphate (LFP) chemistry, with capacities of 53.5 kWh and 66.8 kWh. Smart features are another area where Beijing Hyundai has stepped up its focus for the Chinese market. The Ioniq V features a 27-inch 4K display, Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8295 chip and a head-up display. Its driver-assistance system was jointly developed by Beijing Hyundai and Momenta (HKEX: 6880), providing L2+ assisted-driving functions on highways. The vehicle's infotainment system also integrates AI models including Baidu's Ernie Bot and ByteDance's Doubao, highlighting Hyundai's growing use of Chinese technology suppliers. The rollout of the Ioniq V will serve as the first major market test of Hyundai's latest China strategy. Hyundai officially introduced the Ioniq brand to China in April and plans to launch 20 battery electric vehicle (BEV) and EREV models in the country over the next 5 years. The company aims to scale its China business to 500,000 units by 2030 through faster local development, deeper cooperation with Chinese suppliers and a new generation of electrified products.
